definition: A point in a loss landscape that is a local minimum along some directions and a local maximum along others, rather than a true minimum or maximum.
details: Saddle points are now understood to be far more common than poor local minima in the high-dimensional loss landscapes of deep neural networks, and can slow down gradient-based optimization even though they aren't true minima.

explainer.lead: A saddle point is a point in a loss landscape that is a local minimum along some directions and a local maximum along others, rather than a true minimum or maximum. It matters because such points are far more common than poor local minima in high-dimensional deep network loss landscapes and can slow gradient-based optimization.

tiers.eli5: It is like a mountain pass: going one way you are at the bottom, going another way you are at the top.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers treat them as a practical obstacle in gradient-based optimization; a common pitfall is misdiagnosing a stalled training run as a bad local minimum when it is a saddle point.
tiers.paperLevel: A critical point that is a local minimum along some directions and a local maximum along others. Limits: it is not a true minimum or maximum, yet it can slow gradient-based optimization despite not being a minimum.

explainer.example: In a high-dimensional deep network loss landscape, optimization slows at a saddle point that is a minimum along some directions and a maximum along others.
